rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to persevere in truth and seek perseverance from God through prayer.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is urged to persevere and to persist in the cause of truth, and seek perseverance from God with the help of the prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He should leave his enemies' case to the certain Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: He is told to defer the matter of his enemies to the Day of Judgement, which is certain to come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His responsibility is warning, not making people accept faith.
rows.anchor: his only responsibility is to warn them of this Day; to make them accept faith is not his responsibility.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He should admonish Qur’anically those who fear God; those who mock it face the consequences.
rows.anchor: only admonish through this very Qur’ān those who fear God, and if they are making fun of it, they themselves will face its consequences.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bāʾ in bil-ghayb is locative; believers feared God unseen on evidence within themselves and the world and from prophetic teaching.
rows.anchor: is an adverb of place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers feared the Hereafter without seeing it, unlike rejecters who recognize it only once its reality is unveiled.
rows.anchor: merely on the basis of the arguments found in support of it within their own selves and in the world around them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A qalb munīb is a heart that remains turned toward God through happiness or sorrow, hope or despair.
rows.anchor: refers to the heart which remained inclined towards God whether in happiness or in sorrow and whether in hope or in despair.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering Paradise in peace means no regret over the past or fear of the future and permanent security in the promised kingdom; here the wording follows 15:46, whose salutation context differs.
rows.anchor: They will be asked to enter Paradise with peace; they will neither have any regrets of the past nor any fear of the future.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise grants every desire and additional blessings people cannot imagine or ask for, as 32:17 also indicates.
rows.anchor: God will grant them these favours without they expressing any desire for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh should not trust their power: stronger nations were seized by God and could not save themselves.
rows.anchor: many nations have inhabited this area which were much more stronger and mightier but when God seized them, they were not able to save themselves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The histories of earlier peoples teach those with receptive hearts or attentive ears.
rows.anchor: if they have hearts which can understand and ears which can hear, then the anecdotes of these nations have great lessons for them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The certain Judgement and resurrection are assured because God was not wearied by creating the heavens and earth; the caller will summon people from their graves.
rows.anchor: The Day of Judgement is certain to come. Weariness has not overcome God after creating heavens and the earth so that He will not be able to recreate man.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should patiently endure opposition and diligently maintain prayer.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) should bear with patience and diligently adhere to the prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not to compel belief; he should convey God’s warning through the Qur’an to those willing to hear.
rows.anchor: It is not his responsibility to forcibly make people believers. On the contrary, he should inform of God’s warning through this Qur’ān those who want to get informed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning says Quraysh must not let strength produce pride or confidence that harm cannot reach them.
rows.anchor: their power and strength should not mislead them into conceit and pride that no harm can come to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stronger peoples went about the land seeking refuge, and the question about any shelter explains their motive.
rows.anchor: and he went about find a place of refuge in the land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ruined nation loses its influential classes and surviving commoners scatter in search of refuge.
rows.anchor: This is the state of a nation faced with ruin and destruction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah’s people, ʿĀd, and Thamūd were wholly destroyed, while Pharaoh’s elites drowned and survivors scattered after the state system collapsed.
rows.anchor: some of them were completely destroyed by divine punishment like the people of Noah (sws), the ‘Ād and the Thamūd.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The flood and barren land dispersed Sabāʾ survivors; Jewish survivors of plunder and massacre wandered widely, as did people in later Muslim calamities at Baghdad, Cordova, and Delhi.
rows.anchor: The survivors were compelled to seek shelter and refuge in other places because of the barrenness of their lands and because of straitened economic situation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These histories warn contemporary Muslims as well as Quraysh, if they make the effort to learn from them.
rows.anchor: it is not merely the Quraysh who are warned in this verse, we too can learn many lessons from them on the condition that we make the effort.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes read the phrase as describing victorious campaigns across the land, but the author rejects that reading in favor of roaming to find refuge.
rows.anchor: will be totally out of place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disputed verb means roaming to find refuge, as lexicographers and classical Arabic support, and the following question about shelter confirms.
rows.anchor: it is used to roam the land for finding refuge due to fear.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative refers to the briefly mentioned histories of earlier nations, which teach people able to learn or listen attentively.
rows.anchor: The antecedent of the demonstrative pronoun is the anecdotes of pre vious nations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fully alive heart is sympathetic, reflective, and able to learn; losing these abilities makes a person spiritually dead despite bodily life.
rows.anchor: an alive and vibrant heart.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If a heart is not fully alive, attentive listening to a reasonable speaker can still dispel negligence and revive the ability to learn.
rows.anchor: if someone reasonable tells a person something, then he is able to listen to it with attention.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rebukes Quraysh while comforting the Prophet: its leaders are unmoved because their hearts cannot respond and they will not listen.
rows.anchor: if the leaders of the Quraysh are not being touched by the Qur’ ān he is reciting out to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s lack of weariness after creating the heavens and earth assures the Prophet that resurrection will occur and he should endure what opponents say.
rows.anchor: the Almighty has not become tired after creating the heavens and the earth so that He is unable to re-create them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six creation days mean periods of God’s time; the elaborate, purposeful creation is neither accidental nor amusement and entails a Day when its meaning is revealed.
rows.anchor: and thus means periods of time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No weariness means God’s power remains fully intact for re-creation; the wording sarcastically rebukes those who deem it improbable.
rows.anchor: His power and prowess is fully intact. Not the slightest change has come about in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also mocks the Torah’s notion that God rested on the seventh day after creating the heavens and earth in six.
rows.anchor: this verse also expresses scorn at the notion of the Jews mentioned in the Torah that God created the heavens and the earth in six days and rested on the seventh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objections to endure include the denial of resurrection in 50:2–3; this purposeful world will fulfill its end, though dead-hearted people will believe only upon seeing it.
rows.anchor: one example of which is mentioned earlier in verses 2-3 of the sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer is the means of gaining patience amid opposition: reliance on God enables perseverance, and patience itself requires God’s help, as 16:127 says.
rows.anchor: you cannot be patient unless with the help of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tasbīḥ negates what is unworthy of God and ḥamd affirms attributes befitting Him; together they establish sound knowledge of God and ground patience and trust.
rows.anchor: the former has a ring of negation in it and means “to absolve God from things which are against His majesty,” while the latter has a ring of affirmation in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Constant remembrance enlivens and comforts the heart, while designated worship times coincide with cosmic changes that display God’s greatness.
rows.anchor: they are the ones in which some great change takes place in this universe, which reminds a person of the power and greatness of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before sunrise means fajr and before sunset means ʿaṣr; dawn and the sun’s decline display cosmic submission, and Qur’an and Hadith emphasize both prayers.
rows.anchor: the time when the night folds up and the stars prostrate before the Almighty and the dawn of a new day appears.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night glorification refers to ʿishāʾ and tahajjud; tahajjud is voluntary but especially important for cultivating patience.
rows.anchor: There are two prayers of the night: the ‘ishā’ and the tahajjud prayer.

rows.speaker: people
rows.claim: A general interpretation takes glorification after the prostrations to mean praising God after one’s own prostrations.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have interpreted this to mean that after prostrations too, people should glorify

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead takes sujūd as a verbal noun for the sun’s prostration and understands glorification after it as prayer after the sun’s descent or setting.
rows.anchor: after the prostration of the sun there are times of glorifying the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer order reflects religious importance: fajr first, then ʿaṣr, followed by night prayers, with ẓuhr and maghrib after the sun’s prostration; this covers all five prayers.
rows.anchor: the sequence of the prayers is commensurate with their importance and greatness in religion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sujūd for the sun and stars includes stages of descent and setting; ẓuhr, ʿaṣr, and maghrib occur across those stages.
rows.anchor: When it is used for the sun and other stars, then it refers to their setting and descent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel in 20:130 presents the same call to patience and glorification at appointed times; the details are discussed in the commentary on Ṭāhā.
rows.anchor: one example from S ūrah Ṭāhā in which this subject is discussed very clearly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caller is the angel who will sound the trumpet, already announced in 50:20; istimāʿ means listening attentively.
rows.anchor: The summoner refers to the angel who will sound the trumpet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound’s nearness overturns the negligent assumption that the Hereafter is remote; people will hear it from nearby.
rows.anchor: today these negligent people regard all these happenings to be far off and far-fetched

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image, comparable to 44:10, conveys the event’s certainty, terror, and nearness; verse 19 makes the Hereafter imminent by linking it to each person’s death.
rows.anchor: the summoner may summon any time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing the Prophet implies that he should leave indifferent rejecters aside and remain alert for the event, as a sane person should.
rows.anchor: he himself should be on the lookout for its arrival.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second ‘day’ is grammatically appositional to the previous one; the cry is the trumpet, and ḥaqq calls Judgement certain to arrive.
rows.anchor: of this verse is the permutative of the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together, the two verses tell people to await the trumpet’s heralding sound and their emergence from graves.
rows.anchor: people should vigilantly wait for the sound of the trumpet whose shout these people shall hear on that day to herald its advent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates and causes death, an undeniable fact that shows re-creation cannot be difficult for Him.
rows.anchor: it is God Who creates and it He Who gives death, and this is something which no one can deny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because everyone returns to God, alleged deities or intercessors cannot help in the Hereafter when they control neither life nor death.
rows.anchor: when it is God Who gives life and when it is God Who gives death, then this not only necessitates that God is fully capable of creating again but also that everyone will return to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s splitting depicts people emerging from graves; the marked word is an accusative of state, and other Qur’anic depictions compare their rapid appearance to locusts and moths.
rows.anchor: At other places in the Qur’ān, this depiction is made by saying that just as locusts and moths quickly appear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assembly is easy for God, requiring neither elaborate arrangements nor much time and taking only a blink of an eye.
rows.anchor: no one should be misled by the fact that to recover people from the earth God will have to make elaborate arrangements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God knows what opponents say, the Prophet should not grieve but leave their case to God and continue patiently with his task.
rows.anchor: if He knows what they say, the Prophet (sws) should not be sad and leave the matter to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was not appointed to make people believers; he must keep reminding them, and rejecters bear their own consequences.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is only to remind people, and this he should keep doing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah begins by mentioning the Qur’an and closes by affirming it suffices as a reminder; those demanding punishment are left to their fate.
rows.anchor: It began with the mention of the Qur’ ān. At the end, a reminder is sounded again that the Prophet’s responsibility is only to remind and the Qur’ ān suffices as a reminder.
